name: Analytical Gradients
text:
# Analytical Gradients
Also called: Explicit Gradients, Closed-Form Gradients

## Overview
This family encompasses methods that compute gradients of the rendered image with respect to scene parameters (density, geometry, camera) by analytically differentiating the rendering integral or rasterization pipeline, rather than relying on [automatic differentiation](#7151-automatic-differentiation-reverse-adjoint-mode.md) (AD) or finite differences. It solves the high memory overhead and computational inefficiency of reverse-mode AD, which requires storing $O(kn)$ intermediate states for $n$ pixels and $k$ samples [S5]. By inverting the order of operations or deriving closed-form derivatives, these methods reduce memory consumption to $O(n)$ and provide exact gradients where the underlying operations are differentiable [S5].

## Shared principles
The core mechanism relies on the chain rule applied to the continuous components of the rendering equation. For volume rendering, this involves differentiating the [emission-absorption model](#927-emission-absorption-model.md):
$$
\hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum_{i=1}^N T_i (1 - \exp(-\sigma_i \delta_i)) \mathbf{c}_i
$$
where $\sigma_i$ is density, $\delta_i$ is step size, $\mathbf{c}_i$ is color, and $T_i$ is transmittance [S1]. The gradient $\frac{\partial \hat{C}}{\partial \sigma_k}$ for a specific sample $k$ depends on the transmittance up to $k$ and the emission at $k$, as well as the effect of $\sigma_k$ on the transmittance of all subsequent samples [G]. Unlike [Differentiable Volume Rendering via Box Splines](2449-differentiable-volume-rendering-via-box-splines.md) which uses [basis function interpolation](#5581-amr-basis-reconstruction-filter.md), or [Differentiable Volume Rendering with Analytical Gradients](5983-differentiable-volume-rendering-with-analytical-gradients.md) which derives explicit forms for density, this family also includes [Analytical Derivative of Rendering (Mesh)](6761-analytical-derivative-of-rendering-mesh.md) which applies similar principles to mesh rasterization. A key shared constraint is that discrete steps (e.g., triangle selection, voxel traversal order) are generally non-differentiable and must be handled via masking or fixed selection [S1, unofficial].

## Subtopics

### [Differentiable Volume Rendering via Box Splines](2449-differentiable-volume-rendering-via-box-splines.md)
Computes gradients for volumes defined by box splines using an adjoint transform. It supports 2D/3D [uniform grids](#920-uniform-grid.md) with interpolation orders 0, 1, and 2. It is chosen for geometry calibration in tomography where explicit ray-traced geometry gradients are required [2449].

### [Differentiable Volume Rendering with Analytical Gradients](5983-differentiable-volume-rendering-with-analytical-gradients.md)
Derives explicit analytical forms for radiance transfer with respect to volume density. It avoids the overhead of propagating gradients through long computational graphs inherent in AD. It is chosen for density optimization where basis function interpolation is not used [5983].

### [Analytical Derivative of Rendering (Mesh)](6761-analytical-derivative-of-rendering-mesh.md)
Computes exact gradients for mesh rendering by differentiating the continuous rasterization steps (projection, [barycentric interpolation](#9603-barycentric-interpolation.md), shading). It operates on explicit triangle meshes. It is chosen for geometry and material optimization in mesh-based rendering, though it yields zero gradients for occluded triangles [6761].

## Background
The need for analytical gradients in volume rendering arose from the prohibitive memory costs of standard reverse-mode AD, which stores all intermediate transmittance and radiance values [S5]. Early differentiable volume renderers relied on AD [G]. The explicit formulation for density gradients was introduced to enable efficient optimization of large-scale volumetric data [5983]. The box spline approach extended this to support smooth, continuous volume representations with exact geometric derivatives [2449]. The mesh variant applies similar analytical differentiation to the rasterization pipeline, a concept pioneered in differentiable rendering for computer graphics [6761].
